splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: The circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate an employer's withdrawal liability from a multiemployer pension plan to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether the actuary retains discretion to select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected before the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary retains discretion to select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: The circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects how federal courts calculate sentencing at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that courts lack authority to toll supervised release terms absent explicit statutory authorization, and the term expires as set in the judgment regardless of absconding.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: The circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) against raising any claim previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, in addition to the separate requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended for successive collateral attacks.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically barring them from re-raising any previously presented claim.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of showing newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law, without the additional categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received up to two weeks after Election Day.
splits.description: The circuits disagreed on whether and under what circumstances candidates have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state voting rules. The case raises questions about whether candidates face a cognizable competitive injury from rules that may affect vote counting, with implications for challenges to mail-in voting deadlines and other election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Standing exists
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules that allegedly create competitive disadvantages, even before an election takes place.

positions.label: Standing does not exist
positions.summary: Holds that candidates lack Article III standing for pre-election challenges to ballot-counting rules because the alleged injuries are too speculative or generalized.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits disagreed on the standards for evaluating discrimination claims against business operators, including issues of liability and available remedies. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach, indicating a potential circuit split on the applicable legal framework for fair treatment in hospitality, retail, and service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that business operators face broader liability for discrimination claims, with more expansive remedies available to aggrieved customers.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards apply to discrimination claims against business operators, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions that affect criminal liability or sentencing enhancements.
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether lenity trumps deference to agency interpretations in criminal contexts. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while the Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity. The issue has taken on greater significance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over Auer/Kisor or Chevron deference when interpreting ambiguous provisions that expand criminal liability or sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous provisions when the agency's reading is reasonable.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (requiring only one).
splits.description: The circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) or whether possessing any one is disqualifying. This split affects whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums, with significant liberty implications and sentencing disparities depending on circuit.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: The circuits split on whether Application Note 1 to the career-offender guideline, which adds conspiracy and other inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and defers to the Sentencing Commission's inclusion of conspiracy and other inchoate offenses as 'controlled substance offenses.'

positions.label: Guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) is unambiguous in not including inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline's scope beyond its text, so no deference is warranted.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines even if the substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies. This affects base offense levels and career-offender status for defendants with prior state convictions involving substances not on the federal schedule.

positions.label: State schedule controls — no federal match required
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines broadly includes offenses under state law, even if the particular substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Federal schedule controls — substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance involved is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: The circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in law can be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction under the compassionate release statute. Some circuits hold such changes can never qualify, while others allow courts to consider them, particularly after the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can never qualify
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may qualify
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly when they result in unusually long sentences that would not be imposed today.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for violations of supervised release when revoking supervised release and imposing a new sentence.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether punishment is a permissible purpose when sentencing a defendant upon revocation of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit allows courts to expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences should primarily serve the purposes of deterrence and protecting the public, not retribution.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations when imposing revocation sentences under 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should serve the limited statutory purposes of deterrence and protection of the public, and that courts may not impose sentences primarily to punish for the violation itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed under habeas corpus or may bring claims under other statutory vehicles such as Bivens or the APA.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for prisoners challenging decisions that affect the conditions or terms of their confinement but do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment. The Supreme Court left this question open in Preiser v. Rodriguez, and the lower courts have reached irreconcilable conclusions, particularly in the context of BOP decisions on matters like First Step Act time credits and prerelease custody transfers.

positions.label: Habeas is available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is available (and sometimes exclusive) for prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement that impose additional restraints making custody illegal.

positions.label: Non-habeas remedies available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners challenging conditions of confinement (rather than the fact or duration of imprisonment) may proceed under civil rights statutes or the APA rather than habeas corpus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to orders resolving Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees in criminal cases.
splits.description: The circuits split on whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is the 30-day civil deadline or the 14-day criminal deadline. The majority view treats the motion as a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, applying the civil deadline, while a minority applies the shorter criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case, the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted in good faith to Chapter 7.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether post-petition appreciation in property value becomes part of the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A). The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation inures to the estate, while other circuits have held it belongs to the debtor, creating a split on the scope of 'property of the estate' upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a)'s definition of property of the estate.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity belong to the debtor, not the estate, consistent with the statute's purpose of encouraging Chapter 13 reorganization by protecting debtors who convert in good faith.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal medical records in litigation is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The circuits appear to disagree on whether orders denying motions to seal documents containing private medical information constitute collateral orders that are immediately appealable under 28 U.S.C. § 1291. The D.C. Circuit held that medical privacy is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, but this approach may conflict with other circuits' more restrictive views on the collateral order doctrine's application to sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because the interest can be adequately vindicated through other means or on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
